chapter_title: Advanced Class Features: Inheritance and Polymorphism

screens.title: Inheritance and Polymorphism — Building Flexible Class Hierarchies
screens.subtitle: How classes share behavior and adapt at runtime using virtual functions and abstract interfaces

narration.text: In this lesson we explore two central tools of object-oriented design in C++: inheritance and polymorphism. You will see how a base class can define shared data and behavior, and how derived classes reuse and customize that behavior to model real-world relationships like an Animal and its Dog or Cat specializations. We'll also dig into how virtual functions make the program decide at runtime which override to call, why an abstract class defines a contract with pure virtual functions, and why virtual destructors matter for safe cleanup. Along the way we'll practice a small lab: implement a Shape interface, derive Circle and Rectangle, store them in a vector of Shape pointers, and observe polymorphic dispatch when calling getArea. Finally, we'll call out common mistakes — forgetting virtual on a destructor and assigning derived objects to base objects — and show how to avoid them. By the end you will understand both the code patterns and the practical trade-offs involved in designing a clean inheritance hierarchy. Think about a real system you might model with shared behaviors and how you would use a base class to capture those commonalities.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Inheritance lets classes reuse behavior; polymorphism lets different classes respond differently to the same call based on actual type.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives guide the hands-on lab. First, you will be able to explain what inheritance is and why it helps us reuse code. That means identifying base and derived classes and recognizing an "is-a" relationship like Dog is an Animal. Second, you'll implement single inheritance using base and derived classes so you can move common state and behavior into a shared base rather than duplicating it across types. Third, you'll practice method overriding: giving derived classes their own implementation of a function declared in a base class so specialized types behave correctly. Finally on this screen, you will understand access modes — public, protected, and private — and how they change member visibility for derived classes. Each objective ties directly to the lab tasks you will complete, and to practical design choices you will make when modeling domains in C++.

keyIdea.title: What to practice
keyIdea.text: Be ready to design a base class, derive specialized classes, and move shared code into the base for reuse.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Hands-on goals for polymorphism and safe cleanup

narration.text: These additional objectives prepare you for the lab exercises and safety checks that protect programs at runtime. First, you will define polymorphism and distinguish compile-time from run-time polymorphism by observing when calls are resolved at compile time versus when a virtual function leads to dynamic dispatch. Second, you'll implement run-time polymorphism using virtual functions and abstract classes so derived types can be treated uniformly through base pointers or references. Third, you will practice making base destructors virtual to ensure proper cleanup when deleting derived objects through base pointers, and you will see why this is important to avoid leaking derived resources. Fourth, you'll learn the slicing problem: why assigning a derived object to a base object copy removes the specialized parts and how to avoid that by using pointers or references instead. These objectives guide the practical checks you'll perform in the Shape and Animal labs.

keyIdea.title: Lab focus

narration.text: Inheritance is a mechanism that lets a class acquire properties and behaviors from another class. In the chapter's terms, a derived class inherits from a base class, forming an "is-a" relationship: a Dog is an Animal, and therefore it shares whatever the Animal class provides. Practically, you put common data and functions into the base so multiple derived classes can reuse them rather than duplicating code. For example, name and age belong on Animal because every specific animal has those properties. The derived class then adds its own fields, such as breed for Dog, and can also override behaviors to specialize them. One important detail is member accessibility: derived classes can access base class public and protected members but not private members. This preserves encapsulation while still enabling reuse. A common misconception is to overuse inheritance for code reuse when composition would be simpler; inheritance models a true "is-a" relationship, not just reuse. Before inheriting, ask whether the derived type truly is a subtype. As a quick check, if you can substitute the derived type wherever the base is expected and behavior still makes sense, inheritance is appropriate. Consider small examples you know and decide whether the relationship is substitutional or merely sharing behavior.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Inheritance enables a derived class to reuse and extend a base class, modeling an "is-a" relationship while preserving encapsulation.

content.html:
Definition
Inheritance explained
A derived class acquires public and protected members of a base class. Use inheritance when the relationship is truly "is-a" so polymorphism and substitution make sense.
Why it matters
Centralizing shared behavior reduces duplication, eases maintenance, and clarifies intent when types share common responsibilities.
Common misconception
Inheritance is not a catch-all for reuse. If you only need to reuse implementation, composition may be a better choice to avoid tight coupling.
Concrete example
Animal holds name and age; Dog inherits them and adds breed and fetch(), reusing the Animal constructor and methods.
Key Takeaway

Use inheritance to represent a substitutable subtype that shares behavior and can be treated as the base type when needed.

Hierarchy
Visual: simple hierarchy
Animal (name, age) → Dog (breed, fetch) and Cat (mood, purr). Derived classes reuse Animal members and can override behavior.
Check your understanding
  • Can you substitute a Dog where an Animal is expected?
  • Which members are inaccessible to the derived class?
  • When might composition be preferable?
Tip: Favor clear substitution semantics; test with simple examples before adding complex inheritance trees.

screens.title: Access Modes: public, protected, private
screens.subtitle: How inheritance changes member visibility and the effect on design

narration.text: Access modes determine how base class members appear to derived classes and to outside code. In public inheritance — the most common — public members stay public and protected members remain protected in the derived class. This preserves the intended interface and the "is-a" relationship. With protected inheritance, both public and protected members of the base become protected in the derived class, effectively hiding the base's public interface from outside users while still allowing derived classes to use the members. Private inheritance converts public and protected members of the base into private members in the derived class, which usually indicates a "has-a" or implementation-using relationship rather than a true subtype. To decide which mode to use, ask whether external code should treat the derived as a base; if yes, use public inheritance. A common error is to use private inheritance when you actually need polymorphism; private inheritance prevents substitution by outside code. Another practical detail: private members of the base are never directly accessible to derived classes; they remain hidden, protecting internal invariants. When you design a class hierarchy, pick the access mode that reflects how clients should interact with your derived type, and prefer public inheritance for subtype relationships that require polymorphic behavior.

keyIdea.title: Accessibility rule
keyIdea.text: Public preserves the base interface; protected hides it from outside code but keeps it for derived types; private hides it even from further subclasses.

content.html:
Access Modes
How public, protected, and private affect derived classes
Public inheritance
Public stays public; protected stays protected. Use this for true "is-a" relationships and polymorphism.
Protected inheritance
Public and protected become protected in derived; outside code cannot use the base interface through the derived type.
Private inheritance
Public and protected become private. This is closer to implementation reuse than a public subtype.
Examples & checks
Design check
If external users should call base methods through derived objects, choose public inheritance; otherwise, consider protected or private.
Misuse example
Using private inheritance when you intend polymorphism prevents base pointers from referring to derived objects, defeating run-time dispatch.
Key Takeaway

Pick the access mode that matches your intended external API: public when the derived is substitutable for the base.

screens.title: Method Overriding and the override keyword
screens.subtitle: How derived classes replace base behavior safely

narration.text: Method overriding is how a derived class provides a new implementation for a function already declared in its base class. This is fundamental to making specialized types behave differently while keeping a common interface. In C++ you declare the base method (optionally virtual) and then define a method with the same signature in the derived class. A practical tip from the chapter: use the override specifier in the derived method. It doesn't change behavior at runtime, but it helps the compiler catch errors when the derived signature doesn't match the base signature, preventing accidental overloading rather than overriding. Consider a base makeSound method and a Dog override: when declared virtual in Animal and overridden in Dog, calling makeSound on an Animal pointer to a Dog object triggers the Dog version at runtime. A common misconception is assuming override is required; it is optional but strongly recommended because it enforces intent. Another pitfall is mismatched signatures — the compiler will silently create a new overload if the signatures differ, and your polymorphism will silently fail. Always prefer explicit override to catch that error. In practice, write small tests that call base pointers to confirm the derived behavior is dispatched.

keyIdea.title: Override safely
keyIdea.text: Use override in derived classes so the compiler verifies you intended to override a base virtual function and avoids silent mistakes.

content.html:
Override
Replacing base behavior with derived code
When a derived class implements a method with the same signature as a virtual base method, the derived implementation overrides the base for polymorphic calls.
Misconception
Not using override can turn a misspelled or mismatched signature into an accidental overload, hiding the intended polymorphism.
Key Takeaway

Declare override on derived methods to have the compiler confirm your intent and prevent subtle bugs.

Quick code snapshot
// Base
class Animal {
public:
  virtual void makeSound() const {
    // default
  }
};

// Derived override, safer with override specifier
class Dog : public Animal {
public:
  void makeSound() const override { // compiler checks this really overrides
    // Dog-specific sound
  }
};
Read the code to confirm signatures match. If they don't, override triggers a compile error, saving debugging time.

screens.title: Virtual Functions and Run-time Polymorphism
screens.subtitle: Late binding: choosing the right implementation at runtime

narration.text: Virtual functions enable run-time polymorphism by allowing the program to pick the correct method implementation based on the actual object type at runtime. When a function is declared virtual in the base class and overridden in derived classes, calling that function through a base pointer or reference results in the derived implementation for the actual object. This is late binding because the decision is deferred until runtime. The chapter contrasts this with early binding: without virtual, calls through a base pointer use the base implementation, resolved at compile time. A concrete example is an Animal pointer that points to a Dog object; when makeSound is virtual, calling makeSound on the pointer produces the Dog sound. Practically, use virtual for methods that you intend to override and call polymorphically. Be mindful of performance costs in hot loops, but prefer clarity and correctness first. Also, virtual alone isn't enough; you must use pointers or references for polymorphism to work — storing derived objects by value in base objects causes slicing and loses dynamic behavior. Finally, avoid making everything virtual; pick the methods that form a polymorphic contract. As a learning task, create base pointers to several derived objects and call the virtual method to observe different outputs from a single interface.

keyIdea.title: Run-time dispatch
keyIdea.text: Declare virtual in the base and call through pointers or references so the runtime selects the right overridden implementation based on the actual object type.

content.html:
Concept
Virtual functions and late binding
A virtual function lets the runtime choose the derived override when you call via a base pointer or reference. This is how different types respond to the same message.
Concrete example
Animal* a = &myDog; a->makeSound(); will call Dog's makeSound if it's virtual in Animal and overridden in Dog.
Common mistake
Forgetting to use pointers or references leads to slicing, so virtual dispatch won't occur when storing objects by value.
Quick trial
Animal* a = new Dog("Rex", 2, "Shepherd");
a->makeSound(); // Calls Dog's implementation because makeSound is virtual
delete a; // With virtual destructor, both Dog and Animal destructors run
Try this in the lab using a vector of Animal* to see multiple derived types respond through the same pointer type.

screens.title: Virtual Destructors: Why they matter
screens.subtitle: Ensuring correct cleanup when deleting through base pointers

narration.text: A critical but sometimes overlooked detail in polymorphic hierarchies is the destructor. If you delete a derived object through a base class pointer and the base destructor isn't virtual, only the base destructor runs. That means any cleanup defined in the derived destructor — closing files, freeing memory, releasing resources — will be skipped. The chapter emphasizes: make the base destructor virtual if objects might be deleted polymorphically. This ensures the derived destructor runs first, followed by the base destructor, allowing orderly cleanup of derived resources. Consider a Logger base and a FileLogger derived class: if FileLogger closes files in its destructor but the base destructor is non-virtual, deleting via a Logger* will leak or keep file handles open. Another practical point: adding a virtual destructor incurs negligible cost and avoids subtle resource errors. A common misconception is that destructors are always invoked properly; in polymorphic contexts they are not unless declared virtual. In the lab, allocate a derived object dynamically and delete it through a base pointer to confirm both destructors execute when virtual is used. This small design rule prevents hard-to-find bugs in systems that rely on polymorphism.

keyIdea.title: Destructor rule
keyIdea.text: If a class is intended to be a polymorphic base, declare its destructor virtual so derived cleanup runs correctly when deleted through base pointers.

content.html:
Safety check
Declare virtual destructors for polymorphic bases
A virtual destructor ensures derived destructors are invoked when deleting through a base pointer, preventing resource leaks.
Risk
Without virtual, derived cleanup is skipped when deleting via base pointers — a common source of leaks.
Key Takeaway

When a class is used polymorphically, make its destructor virtual to guarantee proper destruction order.

Code reminder
class Animal {
public:
  virtual ~Animal() { std::cout << "Animal destructor" << std::endl; }
};

class Dog : public Animal {
public:
  ~Dog() override { std::cout << "Dog destructor" << std::endl; }
};

// delete through Animal* calls Dog then Animal when destructor is virtual
Try removing virtual to see only the base destructor run — observe the difference in cleanup output during the lab.

screens.title: The Slicing Problem
screens.subtitle: Why assigning derived objects to base objects loses specialized data

narration.text: Slicing happens when you assign a derived class object to a base class object by value. The derived-specific parts are not part of the base subobject copy, so they are ‘‘sliced off." This is not a compiler bug but a consequence of value semantics: the base object can only hold the members it defines. The chapter warns that slicing defeats polymorphism because the copied object behaves purely as a base object thereafter. A typical mistake is creating a base object from a derived object and then expecting overridden behavior to persist. To avoid slicing, use pointers or references when you need polymorphic behavior: a base pointer can point to any derived object without losing specialized data. In container code, prefer storing pointers or smart pointers in vectors if you need polymorphism; storing objects by value will slice. Another subtle point is copying: copying via a base reference still preserves the dynamic type if you copy the pointer or reference, but copying into a base object does not. When designing APIs, document whether parameters are by value or by reference to prevent accidental slicing. In the lab, try assigning a derived object to a base object and observe the results to internalize why pointers are essential for polymorphism.

keyIdea.title: Slicing summary
keyIdea.text: Slicing removes derived parts when copying into a base object; use pointers or references to preserve dynamic type and polymorphic behavior.

content.html:
Pitfall
The slicing problem
Assigning a derived object to a base object by value copies only the base portion. The derived members and behavior are lost in the copy.
Practical consequence
Polymorphism disappears because the copied object is now a plain base object, not the original derived type.
Avoidance

Use base pointers or references, or smart pointers in containers, to preserve dynamic type and behavior.

Try this
Dog d("Buddy",3,"Retriever");
Animal a = d; // slicing: a now contains only Animal part
// a.makeSound() calls Animal's version — derived behavior is lost
Prefer: Animal* p = &d; p->makeSound(); to preserve polymorphism.

screens.title: Animal and Dog: Constructors, Overrides, and Destructors
screens.subtitle: Step through a working example demonstrating inheritance and polymorphism

narration.text: Let's walk through the Animal and Dog example provided in the chapter to see constructors, overriding, and destructors in action. The Animal base holds protected members name and age so derived classes can use them directly while outside code cannot. Its makeSound is declared virtual to allow derived overrides. The Animal constructor initializes name and age and prints a message to show construction order. Dog publicly inherits from Animal, calls the Animal constructor from its member initializer list, initializes breed, and overrides makeSound, optionally using the override keyword to signal intent. The Dog destructor is declared override as well so the compiler confirms correct signature. When you create a Dog object, the base constructor runs first then the derived constructor; when deleting through a base pointer with a virtual destructor, the derived destructor runs before the base destructor. This order ensures resources owned by the derived are cleaned up first. A common debugging trick is to print messages in constructors and destructors, as the chapter does: it makes object lifetime visible. In the lab, compile and run the example, then change virtual to non-virtual and observe how the behavior differs when calling makeSound through base pointers and when deleting dynamically.

keyIdea.title: Constructor/destructor order
keyIdea.text: Base constructors run before derived constructors; with virtual destructors, derived destructors run before base destructors on deletion.

content.html:
Code
Animal and Dog example
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

class Animal {
protected:
  std::string name;
  int age;
public:
  Animal(std::string n, int a) : name(n), age(a) {
    std::cout << "Animal constructor called for " << name << std::endl;
  }

  virtual void makeSound() const {
    std::cout << "Animal makes a sound." << std::endl;
  }

  virtual ~Animal() {
    std::cout << "Animal destructor called for " << name << std::endl;
  }
};

class Dog : public Animal {
private:
  std::string breed;
public:
  Dog(std::string n, int a, std::string b) : Animal(n, a), breed(b) {
    std::cout << "Dog constructor called for " << name << std::endl;
  }

  void makeSound() const override {
    std::cout << name << " barks: Woof! Woof!" << std::endl;
  }

  ~Dog() override {
    std::cout << "Dog destructor called for " << name << std::endl;
  }
};
Explanation
This code shows protected data, a virtual method, constructor chaining via the member initializer list, and a virtual destructor. Run-time polymorphism is visible when you call makeSound using an Animal pointer to a Dog object. Deleting dynamically allocated Dog objects through Animal* calls the Dog destructor first because the base destructor is virtual.
Guided experiment
  1. Create Animal and Dog instances and observe constructor messages.
  2. Use Animal* to point to Dog and call makeSound(). Note the Dog output.
  3. Delete a dynamically allocated Dog via Animal* and confirm two destructors run in order.
Key Takeaway

Use virtual where you expect polymorphic behavior and always declare virtual destructors for polymorphic bases.

screens.title: Shape Hierarchy Lab: Abstract Class, Circle, Rectangle
screens.subtitle: Hands-on activity to practice pure virtual functions and polymorphism

narration.text: The chapter provides a hands-on lab to implement a Shape hierarchy. The base Shape is abstract: it has a protected color, a parameterized constructor, a pure virtual getArea method, and a virtual displayColor and destructor. Circle and Rectangle publicly inherit from Shape. Each implements its own constructor and getArea. Rectangle also optionally overrides displayColor to add more specific output. The recommended exercise stores Shape* pointers in a std::vector, creates Circle and Rectangle objects dynamically, and iterates over the vector to call displayColor and getArea. This demonstrates run-time polymorphism because the calls dispatch to the actual derived implementations. One important lab step is to delete all dynamically allocated shapes afterward to prevent leaks; this is safe if the base destructor is virtual. Common student mistakes include implementing getArea incorrectly, forgetting to call the base constructor from the derived constructor, or storing objects by value instead of pointers and thereby slicing. In this walkthrough, follow the template code, run the program, and then change one piece at a time — for example make the destructor non-virtual — to observe the effect. These experiments build intuition about abstract classes, pure virtual functions, and safe polymorphic usage.

keyIdea.title: Lab goal
keyIdea.text: Build an abstract Shape base and derived shapes, store pointers in a vector, call virtual methods to see polymorphism in action, and delete safely.

content.html:
Starter code
// Abstract Base Class: Shape
class Shape {
protected:
  std::string color;
public:
  Shape(std::string c) : color(c) { std::cout << "Shape constructor called for " << color << std::endl; }
  virtual double getArea() const = 0; // pure virtual
  virtual void displayColor() const { std::cout << "Color: " << color << std::endl; }
  virtual ~Shape() { std::cout << "Shape destructor called for " << color << std::endl; }
};

// Derived examples: Circle and Rectangle implement getArea()
Follow the lab steps: construct shapes dynamically, push pointers into a std::vector<Shape*>, loop and call getArea and displayColor, then delete pointers and clear the vector.
Lab checklist
  1. Implement Shape with pure virtual getArea and virtual destructor.
  2. Create Circle and Rectangle with proper constructors calling Shape(c).
  3. Use a vector of Shape* to store dynamic objects.
  4. Iterate and call getArea and displayColor to confirm polymorphism.
  5. Delete all objects to avoid leaks and verify destructor order.
Key Takeaway

The lab demonstrates abstract classes as contracts and how virtual functions let multiple shapes respond through a single interface.

screens.title: Assessment & Troubleshooting Checklist
screens.subtitle: Questions and quick fixes for common student errors

narration.text: Before you finish the lab, use this checklist to validate your design and find common mistakes. First, confirm that base methods you meant to override were declared virtual; then call them through base pointers to see dynamic dispatch. Second, check that derived constructors call the base constructor in their member initializer lists so base members are initialized correctly. Third, ensure the base destructor is virtual if you delete derived objects through base pointers; otherwise derived cleanup won't run. Fourth, verify you did not accidentally slice objects by storing derived objects by value in base containers — use pointers or smart pointers in containers instead. Fifth, run the program and observe construction and destruction messages to ensure ordering is as expected: base constructed first, derived constructed next; on deletion, derived destructor runs before base destructor. If a compile error prevents override detection, add the override keyword to the derived signature; the compiler will point out mismatches. Finally, if polymorphism seems not to work, confirm you are using pointers or references and not object copies. Use these checks iteratively while you develop to catch errors early and build robust polymorphic code.

keyIdea.title: Checklist
keyIdea.text: Verify virtual keywords, constructor chaining, virtual destructor, and avoid slicing by using pointers or references in containers.

content.html:
Checklist
Assessment & Troubleshooting
Virtual methods verified
Confirm base methods intended for override are declared virtual and derived methods use override when appropriate.
Constructor chaining
Check derived constructors call the base constructor in the initializer list to properly initialize protected data.
Destructors and cleanup
Ensure the base destructor is virtual when objects are deleted via base pointers to avoid skipped derived cleanup.
Avoid slicing
Store Shape* or smart pointers in containers instead of Shape objects by value.
Quick fixes
  • Add override to derived methods to catch mismatches.
  • Use Animal* or Shape* instead of objects to preserve polymorphism.
  • Make destructors virtual if polymorphic deletion is possible.
Key Takeaway

Run small experiments and check destructor and override behavior to build confidence in your polymorphic designs.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's consolidate the essentials. First, inheritance models "is-a" relationships and enables code reuse by moving shared members into a base class. Second, access modes (public, protected, private) control how base members appear in derived classes and should reflect your intended A P I exposure. Third, method overriding and the optional override specifier let derived classes supply specialized behavior while the compiler helps you avoid signature mismatches. Fourth, virtual functions enable run-time polymorphism so the program chooses the correct override based on actual object type. Fifth, always make base destructors virtual when objects may be deleted polymorphically; otherwise derived cleanup may be skipped. Sixth, abstract classes with pure virtual functions create explicit contracts that derived classes must implement. Finally, avoid the slicing problem by using pointers or references when you need polymorphism. These ideas together let you design flexible, extensible hierarchies that behave predictably at runtime and are safer to maintain.

keyIdea.title: Compact takeaway
keyIdea.text: Combine correct access, virtual design, and pointer-based usage to get safe, flexible polymorphic behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Key Concepts
Key Concepts
Three compact cards summarize what to remember.
Inheritance
Derived classes inherit public and protected members from a base, modeling an "is-a" relationship and enabling reuse.
Polymorphism & virtual
Virtual functions plus base pointers or references allow runtime selection of the correct override for each object.
Safety & pitfalls
Make base destructors virtual and avoid slicing by using pointers or references; prefer override to catch signature errors early.
Summary takeaway
Design hierarchies that reflect substitution, mark virtual methods where needed, and use pointers for polymorphism to keep behavior intact.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Short rules to apply in your code and lab work

narration.text: Keep a few simple rules in mind as you build class hierarchies. First, use public inheritance only when the derived type truly is a subtype of the base and substitution makes sense. Second, declare functions virtual in the base when you expect them to be overridden and called polymorphically, and use override in derived methods to catch errors. Third, always make the base destructor virtual if you will delete derived objects through base pointers. Fourth, avoid copying derived objects into base objects to prevent slicing; prefer pointers or references in containers for polymorphism. These guidelines will make your designs safer, easier to test, and simpler to extend. As you complete the lab, run the experiments suggested in the chapter to see these rules in action so they become reliable habits.

keyIdea.title: Practical rules
keyIdea.text: Public inheritance for true subtypes, virtual for polymorphism, override for safety, virtual destructor for cleanup, pointers to avoid slicing.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › What to Remember
What to Remember
Five practical rules for robust inheritance and polymorphism.
1. Substitution
Only inherit when derived is substitutable for base.
2. Virtual methods
Mark methods virtual in the base when you need runtime dispatch.
3. Virtual destructor
Make the base destructor virtual to ensure derived cleanup.
Final takeaway
These straightforward rules help you design flexible, safe, and maintainable class hierarchies in C++.
